div.head: Section 313
div.p: SOCRATES. What is law? For us, how should we define it?
COMRADE. Which law are you asking about, Socrates?

SOCRATES. What do you mean? Is there a difference between one law and another in respect to being law? Just as gold does not differ from gold in being gold, or a stone from a stone in being a stone, does law differ from law in being law? Or is the nature of law the same everywhere? That is exactly what I am asking: what is law in general?
COMRADE. What else could law be, Socrates, but the things that are accepted by custom and convention?

SOCRATES. Do you think that speech is the things that are spoken, or that sight is the things that are seen, or that hearing is the things that are heard? Or is speech something different from the things spoken, sight different from the things seen, and hearing different from the things heard? In the same way, is law something different from the things accepted by custom, or is it the same?
COMRADE. I now think it is something different.

SOCRATES. Then what would law be? Let us examine it this way: when we see things, what is it that we see them by? By sight. And when we hear things, what do we hear them by? By hearing. Now, when we accept things by custom or convention, what do we accept them by? Is it by law?
COMRADE. Yes.

SOCRATES. But surely sight is not the same as the things seen, nor is hearing the same as the things heard. Therefore, law is not the same as the things accepted by custom. It must be something else, the principle or faculty by which these customs are established. Let us inquire further: what could this be?

div.head: Section 314
div.p: COMRADE. I think law is a resolution or decree of the state.
SOCRATES. You are saying, it seems, that law is a political opinion.
COMRADE. I am.
SOCRATES. Perhaps you are right; but let us examine it this way. Do you call some people wise?
COMRADE. Yes.
SOCRATES. And the wise are wise by wisdom, just as the just are just by justice?
COMRADE. Certainly.
SOCRATES. And the lawful are lawful by law, while the lawless are lawless by lawlessness?
COMRADE. Yes.
SOCRATES. And the lawful are good, while the lawless are bad?
COMRADE. Very true.
SOCRATES. So law, and being lawful, is a good thing, while lawlessness is a bad thing?
COMRADE. That is so.
SOCRATES. Now, is a bad resolution a good thing or a bad thing?
COMRADE. A bad thing, surely.
SOCRATES. But we agreed that law is a good thing. Therefore, a bad resolution cannot be a law, even if it is a resolution of the state.
COMRADE. I agree.
SOCRATES. Therefore, it is incorrect to say simply that law is a resolution of the state, because a bad resolution is not a law. It must be a good resolution.
COMRADE. That seems right.
SOCRATES. And what is a good resolution? Is it not a true opinion?
COMRADE. Yes.
SOCRATES. And a true opinion is the discovery of what is, or reality.
COMRADE. It is.
SOCRATES. So law wishes to be the discovery of what is. When those who make resolutions fail to discover what is, they fail to make a true law, but only an imitation of law.

div.head: Section 315
div.p: COMRADE. But Socrates, if law is the discovery of what is, why do we not all use the same laws for the same things? Since what is remains the same everywhere, should not the laws also be the same everywhere, if they have discovered what is?

SOCRATES. The law still wishes to be the discovery of what is, my friend, but those who do not use the same laws have evidently not always discovered what is. Let us look at it this way. Do we believe that the noble is noble, and the base is base? Or do we believe that the noble is base, and the base noble?
COMRADE. We believe the noble is noble, and the base is base.
SOCRATES. And is this believed only here, or everywhere?
COMRADE. Everywhere.
SOCRATES. And do the Persians also hold this view?
COMRADE. Yes, the Persians too.
SOCRATES. Always?
COMRADE. Always.
SOCRATES. And do people everywhere think that things that weigh more are heavier, and things that weigh less are lighter?
COMRADE. Yes, they think the heavier is heavier, and the lighter is lighter.
SOCRATES. And everywhere do they consider the just to be just, and the unjust to be unjust?
COMRADE. Of course.
SOCRATES. So the things that are reality, that actually are, are recognized as existing everywhere. The things that are not, are not recognized.
COMRADE. True.

SOCRATES. Then the law, if it is true, is the same everywhere. It is the discovery of what is. But perhaps you will object, pointing to the differing customs of mankind. For instance, you might say that we do not believe in human sacrifice, but the Carthaginians do, and consider it a holy law. Or that the customs regarding the burial of the dead differ greatly between the Greeks and other nations.

div.head: Section 316
div.p: COMRADE. Indeed, Socrates, that is exactly what I mean. If you look at the different nations, you see that they hold completely different things to be lawful and unlawful. Even among ourselves, the laws change. What was considered lawful in the past is often unlawful now, and what is lawful now may be unlawful in the future. How can law be the discovery of what is, when it is so variable?

SOCRATES. Because, my good friend, while the things themselves—the realities—do not change, human beings often fail to discover them accurately. Let me ask you: in medicine, do the writings of the doctors concerning health differ, or are the true rules of health the same for all?
COMRADE. The true rules of health are the same for all.
SOCRATES. And those who know these rules are the doctors?
COMRADE. Yes.
SOCRATES. And do the doctors write down different laws about health, or do they agree upon the principles that are truly healthy?
COMRADE. They agree.
SOCRATES. And in farming, do the farmers agree upon the rules for planting and harvesting?
COMRADE. Yes.
SOCRATES. And the writings of these experts—the doctors and the farmers—are their laws concerning their respective arts?
COMRADE. Exactly.
SOCRATES. So whose writings are the laws concerning the administration of the state and the management of people? Are they not the writings of those who know how to rule?
COMRADE. They are.
SOCRATES. And who knows how to rule? Are they not the statesmen and the kings?
COMRADE. Yes.

SOCRATES. So these so-called laws are the writings of the kings and good men. And just as in medicine or farming, those who possess knowledge do not write one thing today and another tomorrow about the same subjects, nor do they write differently from other experts. They discover what is, and they write it down as a permanent law.

div.head: Section 317
div.p: COMRADE. This is true.

SOCRATES. Then if you see some people continually changing their laws, decreeing one thing now and another later, or differing from one another, would you say they possess the true knowledge of what is?
COMRADE. I would say they are ignorant.

SOCRATES. Because the true law, the discovery of what is, does not change. So, the laws of those who truly know are constant and universal. Now, let us consider who among the ancients was considered the best lawmaker, whose laws have remained unchanged for the longest time.
COMRADE. I do not know, Socrates.
SOCRATES. Do you not know whose laws are the most ancient among the Greeks?
COMRADE. Do you mean the laws of the Spartans and Lycurgus?
SOCRATES. The laws of the Spartans are indeed ancient, but there are older laws still. Where did the Spartans get their laws from?
COMRADE. From Crete.
SOCRATES. And who was the most ancient and greatest king of Crete, who gave them these laws?
COMRADE. Minos, the son of Zeus.

SOCRATES. That is right. Minos and his brother Rhadamanthys. But Minos was the elder and the greater. And Homer says of Minos that he was a familiar friend of Zeus, and that he received his laws directly from Zeus. For Homer says: "There is the great city of Cnossus, where Minos ruled as king for nine years, he who conversed with great Zeus."

div.head: Section 318
div.p: COMRADE. But Socrates, if Minos was such a great and good lawgiver, why has he such a bad reputation among the Athenians? They say he was cruel, harsh, and tyrannical, especially concerning the tribute of the seven youths and seven maidens sent to the Minotaur.

SOCRATES. Ah, my friend, that is the peril of making enemies with a city that has a voice and literature, as Athens does. Minos made war upon Athens, and the Athenians, who possessed tragic poets, took revenge upon him in their poetry. They portrayed him as a villain and a tyrant. But if we want to know the truth about him, we should not ask the tragic poets, but the ancient accounts and the poets who spoke the truth, like Homer and Hesiod.
COMRADE. What do they say about him?
SOCRATES. I have already quoted Homer, who says he was the familiar friend of Zeus. Now, do you think Zeus would make a wicked and unjust man his familiar friend?
COMRADE. Surely not.

SOCRATES. And Hesiod says the same thing. He praises Minos as a great and just king. Furthermore, the laws of Minos have remained unchanged in Crete, and the Spartans adopted them because they recognized their excellence. A lawgiver whose laws stand the test of time and bring order to a people is a true discoverer of what is.

div.head: Section 319
div.p: SOCRATES. Consider this: the tragic poets in Athens, who are always looking for a good villain, chose Minos because of the ancient enmity between our city and his. But Rhadamanthys, his brother, they praise as a just judge in the underworld. Yet both were educated by Zeus, and both administered the laws of Zeus. But Minos was the king, the one who established the laws, while Rhadamanthys only carried them out. To be a familiar friend of Zeus means to be educated by him. For Zeus is the greatest of sophists, the greatest teacher of virtue. Minos went into the cave of Zeus every ninth year to learn the laws from him, and then he brought them out and established them for the people. This is why his laws are divine and have lasted so long.
COMRADE. But what about Talos, Socrates? The stories say he was a man of bronze who guarded the island of Crete.

SOCRATES. Ah, Talos was also a judge. Minos established him to go around the island three times a year, carrying the laws inscribed on tablets of bronze. That is why he was called the "man of bronze," not because he was literally made of metal, but because he carried the bronze tablets of the law. He enforced the laws of Minos in the countryside, while Rhadamanthys enforced them in the city.

div.head: Section 320
div.p: SOCRATES. So you see, Minos was the greatest of all kings and lawgivers, the one who best discovered what is, and who established true laws for his people, learning them directly from Zeus. The fact that the Athenians hated him and spoke ill of him in tragedies does not change the truth. For the greatest proof of his excellence is that his laws have made the Cretans and the Spartans well-governed and happy for so many generations.
COMRADE. It seems you are right, Socrates. The evidence of his laws is stronger than the tales of the tragic poets.

SOCRATES. Now let us return to our original inquiry. We said that law is the discovery of what is, and that the true laws are the writings of the experts, the good kings and statesmen who know how to rule the souls of men. Just as the writings of doctors are the laws of health for the body, the writings of good kings are the laws of virtue for the soul. And the one who knows best what is good for the soul is the one who can establish the best laws.

div.head: Section 321
div.p: SOCRATES. Now I ask you: what is it that the good lawgiver distributes to the soul to make it better, just as the doctor distributes food and exercise to the body to make it healthy?
COMRADE. I do not know, Socrates.

SOCRATES. But it is a shame for us, if our souls are the most important part of us, not to know what makes them better or worse. We know what benefits the body, but we do not know what benefits the soul! This ignorance is the cause of all our errors in legislation. We must strive to discover this, so that we too may become experts in the law and know how to distribute the proper nourishment and exercises to the souls of men, making them just and virtuous. Only then will our laws be the true discovery of what is, and not mere imitations.
